paragraphs: November 19, 2013: Apple gets final approval from the Cupertino City Council to proceed with building a massive second campus to house the iPhone-maker’s growing army of workers in California. Regarding the company’s new headquarters, which ultimately will be named Apple Park, Cupertino Mayor Orrin Mahoney issues a simple message: “Go for it.”
However, the massive structure — with an innovative circular design that will earn it the nickname “the spaceship” — remains years away from opening, despite Apple’s ambitious schedule.
Apple CEO Steve Jobs didn’t just want a bigger office for his company. He wanted a headquarters that would embody Apple’s ambitions, down to the smallest architectural detail.
The sprawling circular campus now known as Apple Park was one of Jobs’ final obsessions — a $4 billion monument to his belief that great design could transform even the places where people work.

Its spaceship-like ring, enormous curved glass walls and carefully landscaped grounds make it look more like a vision of the future than a corporate office. But Apple Park also revealed the contradictions in Jobs’ legacy: a project built around collaboration that became an emblem of corporate scale, secrecy and excess.
It wasn’t simply where Apple would make its next generation of products. It was a product in its own right, designed to make a statement about the company that built it.

Apple began tentative work on its new headquarters nearly a decade earlier in April 2006. At that time, the company began acquiring land to house its second campus (after the famous Apple HQ at 1 Infinite Loop). Apple also set in motion the hiring of acclaimed British architect Norman Foster.

Along with the iPad, Apple Campus 2 (the project’s original name) became a major focus for Jobs as his health worsened. He was outspoken about many details of the massive construction project, from the materials used to the philosophy of the building, which was designed to promote serendipitous collaboration between employees.
